questions.stem: A client receiving an unfractionated heparin infusion develops hematuria and a falling hemoglobin; the most recent aPTT was markedly supratherapeutic. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue the heparin at a lower rate and administer vitamin K to reverse the anticoagulant effect gradually.","B":"Stop heparin now and prepare for slow protamine administration based on the amount of recent heparin exposure.","C":"Stop heparin and administer four-factor PCC as the specific first-line antidote for unfractionated heparin.","D":"Continue the infusion while transfusing plasma because stopping heparin may worsen the original thromboembolism."}}
questions.rationale: Active bleeding with excessive unfractionated-heparin effect requires stopping the heparin; protamine sulfate neutralizes heparin and is given slowly because serious reactions can occur. Vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonists, 4F-PCC is not the specific antidote for heparin, and continuing heparin during clinically significant bleeding is unsafe.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Heparin Sodium Injection prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Section 10, Overdosage: bleeding; protamine sulfate neutralizes heparin

questions.stem: A prescriber orders IV potassium chloride for a client with hypokalemia. Which action is essential before the nurse administers potassium chloride concentrate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Inject the concentrate intramuscularly to reduce irritation of the peripheral intravenous catheter.","B":"Administer the concentrate by slow IV push while continuously monitoring the cardiac rhythm.","C":"Mix the concentrate in a small syringe and inject it into the closest port of a running IV line over several minutes.","D":"Dilute it in an appropriate IV solution and administer it by a controlled infusion device at the ordered rate."}}
questions.rationale: Potassium chloride concentrate must be diluted before administration and is for intravenous infusion, not direct IV injection. Controlled infusion reduces the risk of fatal hyperkalemia and arrhythmia. IM administration, IV push, and injecting undiluted concentrate into a running line are unsafe.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Potassium Chloride for Injection Concentrate
questions.source_detail: Updated July 1, 2026: concentrate must be diluted; IV infusion only; avoid rapid infusion

questions.stem: A client with HFrEF and a history of bronchial asthma has a new prescription for propranolol. Which action should the nurse take before administering the first dose?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Clarify the prescription because propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker contraindicated in bronchial asthma.","B":"Administer propranolol because any beta-blocker provides the same heart-failure benefit and airway risk.","C":"Hold all beta-blocker therapy permanently because a history of asthma rules out the entire medication class.","D":"Substitute metoprolol without contacting the prescriber because beta1 selectivity completely eliminates bronchospasm risk."}}
questions.rationale: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker whose prescribing information lists bronchial asthma as a contraindication. The prescription should be clarified rather than administered automatically. Asthma does not justify independently discontinuing all beta-blocker therapy or substituting another drug without an order; even beta1-selective agents are not completely beta1-specific and require clinical judgment.
questions.source_detail: Contraindications: bronchial asthma; warning regarding nonallergic bronchospasm

questions.stem: A client who recently started lisinopril reports a persistent dry cough but has no facial swelling, tongue swelling, dysphagia, or dyspnea. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The cough indicates impending laryngeal angioedema and requires epinephrine despite the absence of swelling.","B":"The cough shows the lisinopril dose is subtherapeutic and should be increased before the next blood-pressure check.","C":"A persistent nonproductive cough is a recognized ACE-inhibitor class effect related to bradykinin accumulation.","D":"The cough is unrelated to lisinopril because ACE-inhibitor respiratory adverse effects always include edema."}}
questions.rationale: Persistent nonproductive cough is a recognized ACE-inhibitor class effect, attributed to reduced degradation of endogenous bradykinin. It is distinct from angioedema, which involves swelling and may threaten the airway. The cough does not indicate an inadequate dose, and its absence of swelling does not make a medication relationship unlikely.

questions.stem: A client taking lithium has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days and now has a coarse tremor and confusion. A lithium level obtained 1 week ago was therapeutic. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Give the next lithium dose because a therapeutic level from the prior week excludes current toxicity.","B":"Withhold lithium and obtain an urgent current lithium level, renal-function tests, and electrolyte assessment.","C":"Treat the findings as uncomplicated viral illness and repeat the lithium level later at the next routine outpatient visit.","D":"Double the next lithium dose to replace medication presumed lost through vomiting and diarrhea."}}
questions.rationale: Volume depletion and acute illness can increase lithium-toxicity risk, and gastrointestinal plus neurologic findings such as vomiting, diarrhea, tremor, and confusion are concerning. A week-old therapeutic level does not establish the current concentration. The next dose should be withheld while an urgent current level, renal function, and electrolytes are assessed.
